scenes.author: Piero Scaruffi
scenes.desc: Una visión nostálgica del pop de los sesenta con ritmos y arreglos electrónicos: Stereolab (Transient Random Noise Bursts With Announcements, Mars Audiac Quintet), lenguaje tan austero como la música clásica y tan ligero como el easy-listening; Saint Etienne (Foxbase Alpha, Tiger Bay); State Of Grace, Broadcast y el «hard electronica» de Add N To X. Japón sobresale en el kitsch paródico y futurista: Pizzicato Five, Cibo Matto, Fantastic Plastic Machine, Buffalo Daughter, Cornelius. Y fuera: Air (Moon Safari), Mocket, Komeda, Stereo Total, Beanfield, Le Hammond Inferno.

xref.title: Early Sound System Inadequacy (1972)
xref.body: In 1972, The Grateful Dead held a meeting in their Novato, California, warehouse practice space to discuss the inadequacy of their concert sound. Their system, designed by Bob Hyal in 1968, utilized Alltec's "Voice of the Theater" series cabinets, radial horns (a novel inclusion at the time), ring tweeters, and a custom crossover, and while "better than most," it was deemed "lacking by 1972" for the band's needs.

xref.title: Ambitious Diamond Dogs Tour (1974)
xref.body: The tour supporting the "Diamond Dogs" album was one of the most ambitious and expensive rock had ever seen. It featured elaborate sets, costume changes, choreography, and a cherry-picker boom that took Bowie out over the audience during "Space Oddity." This pushed the basic rock and roll show into unprecedented theatrical territory. "It was hugely expensive and very complex for its day and no one had ever seen anything like it."

xref.title: The Robot Helmets – 1974 Phantom of the Paradise; Air Conditioning; Communication Links; Spider-Man Effects Company
xref.body: The robot mythology was inspired partly by the 1974 Brian De Palma film Phantom of the Paradise, in which disfigured character Winslow Leech wore a helmet to hide his injuries, and partly by a 1970s band called Space, whose members wore helmets and spacesuits for anonymity. The first helmets had wigs (Thomas had curly hair, Guy-Manuel had long straight hair) until on the way to a 2001 magazine photo shoot they decided robots should look bald and ripped out the fake hair. The helmet designs became increasingly ornate: some reportedly had built-in air conditioning and communication links so they could talk to each other and their crew during performances. One set of helmets was made by the same special effects company that worked on one of the Spider-Man movies. The anonymity was so effective they could walk right through crowds at their own shows unrecognized. One impostor ran up a huge bar tab at a club in Ibiza by claiming to be Thomas Bangalter. "People thought the helmets were marketing or something, but for us, it was sci-fi glam."

xref.title: Crash 'n' Burn Club (Summer 1977) – First Punk-Only Venue in Canada, Shut Down by Liberal Party Complaints
xref.body: The Diodes formed in late 1976 in Toronto and opened their first show supporting the Talking Heads in January 1977. That summer, they converted their rehearsal space at 15 Duncan Street in downtown Toronto into Crash 'n' Burn, the first punk-only club in Canada. Numerous young bands from Canada and the US played there over several months until the club's closure in the fall — the cause being that the Liberal Party of Canada had an office upstairs and kept complaining to the landlord about the noise and the strange people outside. The Diodes were the first Canadian band to sign with a major label, inking a deal in August 1977 and releasing their self-titled debut album in October. "The Liberal Party of Canada had an office, and they kept complaining to the landlords."

xref.title: British Airways Lawsuit (1984)
xref.body: The Beastie Boys sued British Airways after the airline allegedly used a sample from their song "Beastie Revolution" (likely referring to "Cookie Puss") in a worldwide commercial without permission. The band won a judgment for $40,000, which marked the first money they ever made from music. They used these funds to rent an apartment and rehearsal space at 99 Christie Street. "The Beastie Boys heard it in New York in the cinema, and sued British airways. It was the first money they ever made out of music."

xref.title: Joining Nirvana (1990)
xref.body: A few months after recording his Harling Talks AD demos, Dave Grohl received a call to audition for Nirvana. Scream had broken up over "girlfriend troubles" while on tour, leaving Dave stranded in Los Angeles. Buzz Osborne of The Melvins, who was idolized by Kurt Cobain, recommended Dave for the open drummer position. Dave flew to Seattle, arriving on Friday, September 21, 1990, and after an informal audition, became a member of the band without any explicit invitation, simply because "they just didn't ask him to leave." "Dave packed his kit into a large cardboard box and boarded a flight for Seattle, arriving on Friday, September 21, 1990."

xref.title: Edwin Left 1997 Solo; Brian Byrne Tape Initially Thrown Out, Then Hired; Edwin Returned 2016
xref.body: I Mother Earth formed when Jagori Tanna and Christian Tanna met Edwin at their shared rehearsal space in 1990, creating a band immediately subject to a major-label bidding war. Edwin left in 1997 to go solo, finishing tour commitments that summer. The following year, auditions began; hundreds of demo tapes arrived, including one from a Newfoundlander named Brian Byrne that was immediately discarded. A mutual friend insisted they look again; Brian got a second chance, got the gig, and served as singer from 1998 to 2003. After a long hiatus, a 2012 reunion brought Brian back; Edwin was invited back again in 2016. Both occasionally share the stage on current tours. "His tape was immediately thrown out."

xref.title: First Zero-G Music Video (2014)
xref.body: OK Go partnered with Russian airline S7 to produce the first-ever Zero-G music video for their song "Upside Down and Inside Out." The video was filmed by flying a plane through a series of extreme parabolic trajectories, creating momentary periods of zero gravity. While Commander Chris Hadfield filmed a Zero-G video in space in 2013, OK Go's video is recognized for being filmed within the Earth's atmosphere. "Ok go teamed with a Russian airline called S7 to create the first ever Zero-G Music video for a song called Upside Down and Inside Out."

xref.title: "Ashes to Ashes" Music Video - £250,000 Cost
xref.body: The music video for "Ashes to Ashes" was exceptionally expensive for its time, costing £250,000. Made before MTV existed, its primary purpose was for distribution to TV shows like "Top of the Pops" to allow artists greater control over their public image, a major gamble for Bowie who had just emerged from a costly legal battle with a former manager. "The centerpiece of the record was ashes to ashes, a song that not only picked up the story of Major Tom from Space Audity, a character that Bowie had introduced ten years earlier, but it was also made into a hideously expensive music video that cost 250,000 pounds."

xref.title: "Get Your Own Riffs" Incident
xref.body: During the recording of their debut album in a communal rehearsal space in Manchester, Oasis repeatedly played the same 10 songs. Other bands in the facility noticed the songs were "eerily similar to some very familiar riffs and melodies." At one point, an unknown band "posted a sign on the door of the Oasis rehearsal room and it read, Get Your Own Riffs." "And at one point, one of the other bands using the facility, and we don't know who, posted a sign on the door of the Oasis rehearsal room and it read, Get Your Own Riffs."

xref.title: 90s Reinvention - Sound and Vision Tour
xref.body: Bowie initiated his 90s reinvention with the "Sound and Vision Tour," a two-stage process beginning with a promise to perform his classic hits—such as "Space Oddity," "Ziggy Stardust," "Rebel Rebel," "Young Americans," "Heroes," and "Let's Dance"—one last time before permanently retiring them. His motivation was to clear away past expectations and start fresh. "The first was something called the Sound and Vision Tour, where Bowie promised to play his old hits one more time and then retire them forever."

xref.body: The band ZZ Top has an asteroid named after them, joining a select group of musicians recognized in space. "Eric Clapton, Brian Wilson, ZZ Topp, Yes, Bruce Springsteen, and Jimmy Page are among those with their own pieces of space rock."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

xref.title: Asteroid
xref.body: Bruce Springsteen has an asteroid named in his honor, a piece of space rock bearing his name. "Eric Clapton, Brian Wilson, ZZ Topp, Yes, Bruce Springsteen, and Jimmy Page are among those with their own pieces of space rock."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

xref.title: Asteroid
xref.body: Jimmy Page has an asteroid named after him, placing him among the musicians recognized with celestial bodies. "Eric Clapton, Brian Wilson, ZZ Topp, Yes, Bruce Springsteen, and Jimmy Page are among those with their own pieces of space rock."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

xref.title: Auctioned Album Advertising Space
xref.body: For their 1986 debut album, "Flaunt It," Sigue Sigue Sputnik controversially auctioned off advertising space between the tracks, and also sold space on the external album artwork to companies like Studio Line (L'Oreal) and ID Magazine, effectively embedding commercials directly into the album. "Not only did studio live from L'Oreal and Id Magazine by space on the external album artwork, but commercials were embedded in the album itself."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

xref.title: Band Name Origin – American History, James Polk's "54-40 or Fight" Manifest Destiny Slogan (1840s)
xref.body: The name 54-40 came from Brad Merritt's stream-of-consciousness naming session in which he generated ideas including "Bridge View Dogs" (after their Surrey rehearsal space area) and "Safeway Rebels." He landed on 54-40, the slogan of US presidential candidate James Polk, who in the 1840s argued that America should take the entire Oregon Territory up to latitude 54°40' North — which included what is now British Columbia, at the time shared with Britain. The two founders had both moved around extensively (Merritt in the US, Osborne across Canada) and had met in high school in Tsawwassen, literally on the US border. "I wanted something which was big and yet small at the same time."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

xref.title: Band Rebirth - Name Change, New Songs, New Rehearsal Space
xref.body: Following a period of struggles and individual pursuits, the band experienced a "rebirth." This was catalyzed by Ian D'Sa bringing in new songs like "Try Honesty" and "Cut the Curtains," Ben Kowalewicz suggesting a band name change (from Pezz to Billy Talent), and acquiring a new rehearsal space. "And then Ben suggested we change the band name and everything just kind of came together all at once and it did feel like a rebirth and we got a new rehearsal space down the front and sure burn over here and we felt like a real band again and was up."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: Billy Talent In Their Own Words: Part 1

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
The Ongoing History of New Music

xref.title: CD vs. Vinyl Era Recording Mentality
xref.body: When recording *Road Apples*, their first CD, the band's approach was still influenced by vinyl. They aimed for "five songs on A, five songs on B" to create their best ten tracks, rather than filling the CD's 60-70 minute capacity. This contrasts with the later trend of artists extending album lengths to maximize CD space. "This was our first foray into, this is the first CD we ever made for road apples... We always thought in five songs on A, five songs on B. And you pick your best ten."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

xref.title: Camden Rehearsal Space
xref.body: The band rehearsed in a building in Camden, which notably featured a jukebox. This jukebox was stocked with the latest singles from contemporary bands like The Ramones, as well as reggae songs from Jamaican artists such as Bob Marley and dub pioneer Lee Scratch Perry. The Clash particularly favored Dub music, identifying it as the music of the immigrant communities with whom they shared their neighborhood. "The clash rehearsed in a building in Camden that featured a jukebox stock with the latest singles from bands like The Ramones and Reggae Songs from Jamaican artists like Bob Marley and Dub Pioneer Lee Scratch Perry."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

xref.title: Classic Rock Covers
xref.body: The Space Lady is known for performing covers of classic rock songs, a characteristic mentioned when introducing a sample of her music. "Susan Dietrich, otherwise known as The Space Lady, and one of her many classic rock covers."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

xref.title: Communal Rehearsal Space Sign
xref.body: During the creation of their debut album in a Manchester communal rehearsal space, Oasis's repetitive playing of songs with familiar riffs and melodies led another unnamed band in the facility to post a sign on Oasis's door, which read, "Get Your Own Riffs." "posted a sign on the door of the Oasis rehearsal room, and it read, Get Your Own Riffs."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

xref.title: Comparison to The White Stripes
xref.body: The Black Keys experienced an increase in interest and profile due to the rising popularity of The White Stripes, another garage-punk two-piece band. The greater success achieved by The White Stripes inadvertently helped to draw more attention to The Black Keys. "The bigger the white stripes got, the more interesting to grow in the black keys."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: Catching Up With The Black Keys

xref.title: Confidence from "Space Oddity" Success
xref.body: The success of "Space Oddity," particularly its high chart position in the UK, provided Bowie with much-needed confidence. This newfound self-assurance encouraged him to be even bolder with his experiments in image and presentation, leading to his iconic gender-bending styles. "This success gave Bowie some much needed confidence. He felt he could even be more bold with his experiments with the image and presentation, which often involves some serious gender bending."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

xref.title: Creation of Ziggy Stardust
xref.body: Building on glam rock concepts, Bowie developed the character Ziggy Stardust. This persona was inspired by the outrageous behavior of Iggy Pop and The Stooges, the artsy "scummy" persona of Lou Reed and the Velvet Underground, the "god-alien" self-perception of Vince Taylor, and the "space travel obsessed" persona of Norman Odom, also known as the Legendary Stardust Cowboy. Bowie combined these influences, changing "Iggy" to "Ziggy" and adopting "Stardust" as the surname. "He invented an entire character completely rooted in glam rock concepts that borrowed from the outrageous behavior of another new friend, Iggy Pop... So Bowie, taking all this information, changed Iggy to Ziggy and adopted Stardust as a surname and thus Ziggy Stardust was born."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: The Surprising History of Glam Rock

xref.title: Creator of "Long Player"
xref.body: Jem Finer, associated with The Pokes, conceived and created a project called "Long Player." This musical composition, utilizing Tibetan singing bowls, is designed to generate music continuously for a thousand years. The performance began on New Year's Eve 1999, is set up in a space along the Thames, and is scheduled to conclude on New Year's Day in the year 3000. "Jem finer of the pokes is the creator of a project called Long Player. Using some Tibetan seeing bowls, he set things up in such a way that these bowls will naturally generate music for a thousand years."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

xref.title: David Bowie's Praise
xref.body: David Bowie openly stated that the Langley kids' version of "Space Oddity" was one of the best interpretations of his songs he had ever heard. This endorsement highlighted the unique charm and sincerity with which the choir performed, despite any technical shortcomings. "And David Bowie went on record as saying that this is one of the best interpretations that he has ever heard of one of his songs."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
The Ongoing History of New Music

xref.title: Dislike of Reality TV Presence
xref.body: Tom Delonge expressed his disapproval of Travis Barker's involvement in reality television, specifically the MTV show "Meet the Barkers," which extensively documented Travis and his wife Shannon Mochler. The presence of TV cameras, even in the Blink-182 rehearsal space, was a source of discomfort for Tom. "Tom also wasn't a fan of Travis getting into the reality TV show game."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: The Rise and Fall and Rise of Blink 182 Part 3

xref.title: Distinctive Style and Rehearsal Space
xref.body: For an added touch of the surreal, The B-52s chose to rehearse in the blood-letting room of an abandoned mortuary, an unconventional choice that underscored their eccentric and offbeat artistic approach. "And for that surreal touch, the B-52s rehearsed in the blood-letting room of an abandoned mortuary."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

xref.title: Early Career and Persona
xref.body: Susan Dietrich, known as The Space Lady, is from Pueblo, Colorado. For many years, she was a street musician, frequently performing in cities like Boston and San Francisco. She was easily recognizable by her unique outfit: a silver plastic helmet adorned with white wings and a flashing light. She initially played the accordion. "She wore a silver plastic helmet adorned with white wings and a flashing light on top. And she played the accordion."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

xref.title: Early Life and Family
xref.body: Timmy Comerford's father was a rocket scientist, specifically an engineer who worked on the space shuttle, while his mother was a mathematician and a teacher. His family life was troubled, marked by his mother's brain cancer diagnosis which led her to move away, a subsequent divorce, a stepmother, and the death of his biological mother in 1988. "His dad was a rocket scientist. Now seriously, a rocket scientist."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
The Ongoing History of New Music

xref.title: Extensive Remix Catalog
xref.body: Depeche Mode is noted for its deep involvement in remixing, to the extent that completists require significant shelf space for their collection. A box set of selected remixes released between 1981 and 2004 contained 37 different remixes of 37 different songs, and another box set released in 2016 featured 28 additional remixes. There's also a vinyl "suitcase-like collection" spanning half a dozen discs, illustrating the band's prolific output of remixed material. "I have on my shelf a box set of selected Dopech Mode Remixes released between 1981 and 2004, 37 different remixes of 37 different songs. And next to it is another box set released in 2016 with another 28 remixes."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

xref.title: Failed Petition for Heavy Metal Element
xref.body: A petition to name a heavy metal element after Lemmy of Motorhead failed. The primary reasons were that scientific rules for naming new elements do not allow for musicians as sources, only mythological concepts, minerals, places, countries, properties, or scientists. Additionally, the new "heavy" elements (113, 115, 117, 118) are actually classified as non-metals on the periodic table. "This petition was inspired by the idea that an actual heavy metal element be named after Lemmy and with atomic weights between 113 and 118, these new elements are the heaviest yet discovered. Perfect. Awesome. Sounds great. However, if we look at the periodic table, you'll see that these new elements occupy space on the right hand side. This is the area of the table reserved for non-metals."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

xref.title: Fascination with Space Program
xref.body: In the late 1960s, Bowie became fascinated by the American space program, particularly influenced by the 1968 film *2001, A Space Odyssey*. He was transfixed by the Apollo program's push towards a moon landing, noting how the Apollo astronauts were worldwide superstars in 1969. This fascination, combined with personal struggles, inspired his song "Space Oddity." "When the Apollo program pushed towards a moon landing, Bowie was absolutely transfixed."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

xref.title: Florence Welch's First Band
xref.body: This punk group was Florence Welch's very first band. Florence played guitar and sang, while her friend Mira played drums. Their practice space was spray-painted with the name of Daniel Johns from Silverchair, a crush of Florence's at the time. "Florence's first band was a punk group called The Toxic Cockroaches."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

xref.title: Formation and Name Origin
xref.body: Layne Staley had been living with a homeless Jerry Cantrell at their rehearsal space when Sleeze, Staley's band, was eventually renamed Alice in Chains. After Staley's other band (a funk outfit) and Cantrell's separate project both broke up, Cantrell and Sean Kinney asked Staley to be the vocalist for their new group, adopting the name of Staley's former band, Alice in Chains, for the new project. "Sleeze was eventually renamed Alice in Chains, while Lane was living with a homeless Jerry Cantrell at their rehearsal space."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: Groups That Changed Their Front-Person and Survived

xref.title: Genre Blending and Influence
xref.body: NoMeansNo occupied a unique space by blending elements of hardcore and metal. Their sound contained elements that would later define post-hardcore, influencing bands like At the Drive-In, Rollins Band, Alexisonfire, Billy Talent, Deftones, and Silverstein. "They ended up occupying a space somewhere between hardcore and metal. If you listen carefully to what they did, you can hear elements of what would become known as post-hardcore, a sound that would later birth groups like at the drive-in, Rollins Band, Alexis on Fire, Billy Talent, The Death Tones and Silverstein."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

xref.title: Geographical Origins and Evolution
xref.body: No Means No originated in Victoria, Canada, and later relocated to Vancouver. Their sound occupied a unique space blending hardcore and metal, and they are recognized for containing elements that would later define post-hardcore. "And then there was no means no, who started in Victoria and later moved to Vancouver. They ended up occupying a space somewhere between hardcore and metal."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

xref.title: Gord Downie's Mementos in Rehearsal Space
xref.body: The band's rehearsal space at The Bath House, which was featured in the "Long Time Running" documentary, contains deeply personal items belonging to Gord Downie, including a mic stand from their final gig, a set list from that show, and his boots, creating what is described as a "pretty sacred sort of spot." "A mic stand from the final tragically-hip gig was standing in Gord Downey's place. On the floor was a set list from the final show. And next to that was a pair of Gord's boots. It's a pretty sacred sort of spot."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

xref.title: Horse Farmer
xref.body: D'Arcy Wretzky, the original bassist for The Smashing Pumpkins, established a horse farm. "Original smashing pumpkin space player Darcy Rezky has a horse farm."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
The Ongoing History of New Music
The Ongoing History of New Music

xref.title: Influence of Norman Odom (Legendary Stardust Cowboy)
xref.body: Norman Odom, a "wacky space travel obsessed Texas singer" known as the Legendary Stardust Cowboy, provided inspiration for the "Stardust" surname and the cosmic elements of Bowie's Ziggy persona. "He also got inspiration from Norman Odom, a wacky space travel obsessed Texas singer who went by the name the legendary Stardust cowboy."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: The Surprising History of Glam Rock

xref.title: Influence on The Black Keys' Growth
xref.body: The Black Keys' career benefited from the concurrent rise of The White Stripes, another prominent "garaji, punky, two-piece band." As The White Stripes gained more popularity, public interest in The Black Keys also grew, indicating a shared musical space and audience appreciation for their raw sound. "The bigger the white stripes got, the more interesting to grow in the black keys."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: Catching Up With The Black Keys

xref.title: Influence on Tom Morello
xref.body: Tom Morello extensively studied old Black Sabbath records, specifically noting how guitarist Tony Iommi demonstrated restraint and utilized the importance of the "space between the notes" in his playing. "He also spent a lot of time listening to old black Sabbath records, noting how guitarist Tony Iomey often exhibited restraint, utilizing that the space between the notes could be as important as the notes themselves."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

xref.title: Inspiration for "Space Oddity" - Stanley Kubrick & Garden Gnomes
xref.body: Bowie was heavily influenced by Stanley Kubrick's "2001, A Space Odyssey," which he saw while "stoned out of his mind" in 1968, leading to the creation of "Space Oddity." The character name "Major Tom" might also have been inspired by Tom Major, the father of future British Prime Minister John Major, who had a second career making garden gnomes. "But it's possible that the name of the character in the song was inspired by the story of a failed British trapezoid artist named Tom Major."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

xref.title: Inspiration for Ziggy Stardust
xref.body: Norman O'Dan, a Texas proto-psychobilly singer also known as The Legendary Stardust Cowboy, was a big fan of space travel and admired by David Bowie. He was one of the two people who inspired the name for Bowie's alien rock star character, Ziggy, in *The Rise and Fall of Ziggy Stardust and The Spiders from Mars*. "And that name was inspired by two people, Bowie's new friend Iggy Pop, and a Texas proto-psychobilly singer named Norman O'Dan, who went by the handle of the legendary Stardust Cowboy."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

xref.title: Intellectual Interests – Reading and Space Race
xref.body: Despite his later reputation, Sid was not unintelligent. He enjoyed reading books by Edgar Allan Poe and followed the American Space Race with significant interest. "He loved reading books by Edgar Allan Poe and watched the American Space Race with great interest."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

xref.title: Inventor of the 12-inch Single
xref.body: Tom Moulton is credited as the inventor of the 12-inch single, an invention he stumbled upon by mistake. Not a DJ or musician himself, Moulton was skilled at extending songs with additional beats. When he ran out of 7-inch blanks while on a tight deadline, he used 12-inch blanks, stretching the grooves to fill the space, resulting in the first 12-inch record. "The inventor of the 12-inch was Tom Molten, and his invention was a mistake."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

xref.title: Isaac Brock's Difficult Youth
xref.body: Isaac Brock, the frontman, experienced a turbulent childhood, including being homeschooled for a period. His mother left his father for his father's brother, and their house subsequently flooded, leading her to move into her husband's trailer. With no space for Isaac, he stayed on the second floor of the flooded house until authorities intervened. "Family life was a little messed up for Isaac. He was homeschooled for a while but then his mum left his father for his father's brother than the house flooded which meant that she had to move into her husband's trailer. But there was no space in the trailer for Isaac so he stayed at the flooded out house on the second floor until the cops made a move."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

xref.title: Jay Semko's Multi-Faceted Career
xref.body: Bass player and singer Jay Semko has pursued a diverse career, composing music for numerous TV series (including "Due South," "Trailer Park Boys" movie, and shows on CBC, Global History Channel, Discovery Channel, APTN, Showcase), performing voiceover work, writing music for museum installations, producing other artists, and releasing at least 11 solo albums. "Space Player and singer J. Senko wrote the music for the TV series Do South. He wrote music for the first trailer park boys movie. He wrote music for the series scene on the CBC, Global History Channel, Discovery Channel, APTN, Showcase, and a whole bunch more. He does voiceover work for radio and TV commercials. He wrote music for museum installations. And he's produced records for other artists, and has at least 11 solo albums."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

xref.title: Joshua Tree Studio Client
xref.body: Daniel Lanois is mentioned as a client of the studio located in Joshua Tree, California. This facility, which serves as both a recording space and the owner's home, was also used by the Foo Fighters for recording their song "Outside." "and Daniel N.Wa."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

xref.title: Late Discovery
xref.body: The speaker, as an older music fan, found himself exploring bands he missed in his youth, such as Spacemen 3, which he discovered having missed them in 1985. "I got into a a Space Man 3 kick for a while. Who's Space Man 3? Again, it just somebody that I discovered that I had missed in 1985."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: OGHONM 1000th Episode: The Q&A From the Live Recording

xref.title: Left-Handed on Right-Handed Kit
xref.body: Stuart Copeland is left-handed but plays a drum kit set up for right-handers, which made his complex rhythms even more distinctive. This playing style has been compared to Ringo Starr, who, despite playing right-handed, frequently led with his left hand for fills and flourishes. As a three-piece band, The Police's structure provided ample space for Stuart Copeland's elaborate drumming. "His rhythms were made all the more complicated because Stuart is left-handed."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: History of the Modern Drum Kit

xref.title: Maria's Hair Design Rehearsal Space
xref.body: The Stiff Woody's, Kurt and Chris's first band, spent a considerable amount of time rehearsing at Maria's Hair Design, Chris's mother's beauty salon. "It's been a lot of time rehearsing at Maria's Hair Design."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

xref.title: Mementos in Rehearsal Space
xref.body: In The Tragically Hip's rehearsal space at The Bath House, a mic stand used during the band's final gig, a set list from that show, and Gord Downie's boots are preserved, creating a "sacred sort of spot" that symbolizes his enduring presence. "A mic stand from the final tragically-hip gig was standing in Gord Downey's place."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: Arkells - In Their Own Words:  Part 2

xref.title: Multiple Mixes of "Battle Flag"
xref.body: In addition to the original album mix and the official radio edit, "Battle Flag" had several other versions, including the "Space Raiders mix," the "Big Beat boutique mix," and a "Low Fidelity All-Stars mix," with another featuring the original writer of the song. This illustrates how numerous remixes could be created for a single track. "In addition to the original album mix, there's something called the Space Raiders mix, the Big Beat boutique mix, another featuring the original writer of the song, and the Low Fidelity All-Stars mix."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

xref.title: MySpace Discovery
xref.body: The band gained attention from numerous record labels after fans began posting their early do-it-yourself recordings on MySpace. This illustrates a shift in how A&R departments scouted new talent, leveraging online platforms. "They came to the attention of a lot of record labels as the result of fans posting their early do-it-yourself recordings to my space."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

xref.title: Name Origin
xref.body: She acquired the name "Space Lady" following some newspaper coverage of her performances. "She got the name Space Lady after some newspaper coverage."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

xref.title: Naming Origin
xref.body: The band Sleater-Kinney was named after a road near their rehearsal space in Olympia. This detail provides a local context for their origins and connection to the Pacific Northwest scene. "Slater Kinney was formed in Olympia and named after Roboad near where the band used to rehearse."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

xref.title: New Young Band Inspired by Classic Rock
xref.body: The Struts, a British band, were highlighted as a new young group "brought up on Queen, Aerosmith Oasis, the killers and the Rolling Stones." This demonstrates a trend of contemporary bands drawing direct inspiration from old school classic rock to create their sound, fitting into the Alternative Hard Rock space. "And we should also pay attention to the struts. A British band brought up on Queen, Aerosmith Oasis, the killers and the Rolling Stones."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: The History of the 2010s Part 4: The Revivals

xref.title: Origin of the Name "Stone Temple Pilots"
xref.body: After two weeks of brainstorming, the band settled on Stone Temple Pilots. The initials "STP" came from an old STP oil treatment can that Scott Weiland had as a "shrine" in his living space, reminding him of a childhood STP sticker on his bicycle and NASCAR driver Richard Petty, who was sponsored by STP. The full words "Stone Temple Pilots" were chosen while the band members were "drunk and stoned" as they sounded the best among many combinations, despite meaning "absolutely nothing." "From there was just a matter of matching up words to the letters."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

xref.title: Owner of Torpedo Comics
xref.body: John Dolmayan, the drummer for System of a Down, is also the proprietor of Torpedo Comics, recognized as one of America's premier comic book stores. Located in Las Vegas, the store operates out of a 3,500 square foot space and has been in business since 2003, specializing in rare comic books. "He's also the owner of one of the best comic book stores in America. It's called Turpedo Comics."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

xref.title: Powerful Bottom End
xref.body: A key element contributing to Rage Against the Machine's distinct sound was their powerful "bottom end," driven by bassist Tim Commerford and drummer Brad Wilk. Singer Zack de la Rocha and guitarist Tom Morello recognized the need to allow the rhythm section ample space to contribute to the band's overall sound. "One of the things that made Rage Against the Machine so cool was that bottom end."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

xref.title: Preference for Thematic Horror
xref.body: Hammett prefers horror movies with supernatural, monster, outer space, or paranormal themes, tending to avoid overtly violent horror. He sees "torture porn" as a "cheap thrill" that often lacks the plot and intrigue he values, making it difficult for him to recognize any artistry in it. "I tend to shy away from horror movies that are overtly violent. You know, I like horror but I don't like horror for the sake of it."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: Kirk Hammett’s Movie Poster Collection ｜ Bonus Podcast

xref.title: Quit Mod Robes, Sought Radio Job
xref.body: After watching the movie "Office Space," Ben abruptly quit his job at Mod Robes. He then contacted George Stroumboulopoulos, seeking advice on how to get a job in radio. "And I remember watching the movie Office Space and then the next day I went into mod robes and I quit. And I called George and I said, hey, I want to get a job at radio. How do I do it? How, where would I start?"

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: Billy Talent In Their Own Words: Part 1

xref.title: Reality TV Show
xref.body: Travis Barker starred in a reality television series called "Meet the Barkers" on MTV. The show documented his life with his wife, Shannon Mochler, even extending to filming inside the Blink-182 rehearsal space, which was a point of contention for Tom DeLonge. "Remember, meet the Barkers? That was an MTV show that followed Travis and his wife Shannon Mochler everywhere, including into the Blink rehearsal space."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: The Rise and Fall and Rise of Blink 182 Part 3

xref.title: Recording Studio in Church Basement
xref.body: The band transformed the basement of their purchased church in Farnham, Quebec, into a fully outfitted recording studio, providing them with a dedicated, cost-effective space to experiment and record without incurring large external studio bills. "The basement was renovated and outfitted with a recording studio."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: Who the Hell is Arcade Fire? Part 1

xref.title: Recording Studio in Tire Factory
xref.body: For their third album, *Rubber Factory*, The Black Keys repurposed the second floor of a former General Tire factory in East Akron, Ohio, renting the space for $500 a month. This unique studio choice highlighted their connection to their hometown's industrial heritage, as Akron was a major tire manufacturing hub, and they even attended Firestone High School. "The third album was recorded in a different spot, and the band-in-tire factory in East Akron that was once run by General Tyre".

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: Catching Up With The Black Keys

xref.title: Recording at Air Lyndhurst Hall
xref.body: Adele was a client at Air Lyndhurst Hall, George Martin's studio in North London, utilizing its large Studio One, a hexagonal space capable of accommodating an entire orchestra and choir. "Clients have included you too, Adele, Kate Bush, Liam Gallagher, Coldplay Muse, and Mumford and Sons."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

xref.title: Recording at St Catherine's Court
xref.body: Due to the lack of toilets at their Kanda Plaas rehearsal space, Radiohead moved to St Catherine's Court, a 14th-century castle in Bath, once owned by Henry VIII and rented out by actress Jane Seymour. The quiet, out-of-the-way location and the acoustics in its ballroom and library made it worth the significant rent of 10,000 pounds per week (or 175,000 Canadian dollars for their two-month stay). "Well, it's just dumb reason, but no one had ever installed toilets at Kandaplas."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

xref.title: Rehearsal Space - The Shed
xref.body: After living in a friend's basement for a while, Isaac Brock built a shack next to his mother's trailer, which they named "the shed." This structure became the primary rehearsal space for Modest Mouse in their early days. "After living in a friend's basement for a while, Isaac built a shack next to the trailer and this became the rehearsal space for modest mouse. They called it the shed."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

xref.title: Saved by the American Space Program
xref.body: The American space program is credited with diverting Bowie from a potential life of photocopying and mime, setting him up to become one of the most important artists of the 1970s. "But the thing that saved Bowie from a life of photocopying in mime abuse was the American space program."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

xref.title: Self-Built Studio and Album Scrapping
xref.body: On February 1, 1996, Radiohead returned to their rehearsal space, Kanda Plaas, an old farmhouse in Sutton Courtney, Oxfordshire. At their manager's insistence, they invested $250,000 in recording gear, intending to save money by no longer renting expensive studios. They wrote and rehearsed extensively, completing an entire album, but then scrapped it, believing they could do better, and started over. "The bank account took a $250,000 hit."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

xref.title: Sound + Vision Tour - Retiring Hits
xref.body: To shed the "baggage" of his past successes and start fresh, Bowie undertook the Sound + Vision Tour, during which he promised to play his old hits like "Space Oddity," "Ziggy Stardust," "Rebel Rebel," "Young Americans," "Heroes," and "Let's Dance" one last time before retiring them forever. His intention was to clear the decks and move forward creatively. "The first was something called the Sound Invision Tour where Bowie promised to play his old hits one more time and then retire them forever."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
The Ongoing History of New Music

xref.title: Space Satellite Name
xref.body: An experimental space satellite weighing 12 kilograms was named "Tori" in her honor. This satellite was designed to explore complex issues of orbital mechanics, and Tori Amos was a significant source of inspiration for its designers. "Tori, which is what it's called, is a 12 kilogram experimental satellite designed to explore the complicated issues of orbital mechanics."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

xref.title: Space and Aeronautics Enthusiast
xref.body: Dave Rowntree developed a lifelong interest in space, astronomy, rockets, and exploration. In 1998, he and bandmate Alex James toured NASA facilities in Houston, an experience that led them to get involved with the European Space Agency's Mars Express mission, for which Blur recorded a musical call sign. "Dave has always been into space, astronomy, rockets, exploration, that kind of thing."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

xref.title: Studio One Facilities and Use
xref.body: Studio One is a massive space, two and a half stories tall, resembling a gigantic gymnasium. It is primarily used for symphonic work and film scores, having hosted a 65-piece orchestra for the final Harry Potter film soundtrack and John Williams' score for *Star Wars*. "Studio One is huge. It's like a gigantic gymnasium, two and a half stories tall."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

xref.title: Taylor Hawkins' Favorite Drummer Ever
xref.body: Roger Taylor was Taylor Hawkins' favorite drummer of all time. This admiration was evident from Hawkins' enthusiastic reaction to a poster of Taylor's solo album "Fun in Space" at the Foo Fighters' studio. "That's Roger Taylor, man. He's my favorite drummer ever."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

xref.title: The Bathouse Recording Experience
xref.body: The band recorded their "Hope and Ruin" album at The Bathouse, The Tragically Hip's studio in Bath, Kingston. This studio is described as an old coach house with a swimming pool, basketball court, grand piano, and living/sleeping quarters upstairs, functioning as a live-work recording space. "It's one of these old-style live work recording studios."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: The Trews: In Their Own Words

xref.title: The Legendary Stardust Cowboy Persona
xref.body: Norman Odom, a "wacky space travel obsessed Texas singer," adopted the stage name The Legendary Stardust Cowboy, from whom David Bowie drew inspiration for the "Stardust" surname in his Ziggy Stardust character. "Norman Odom, a wacky space travel obsessed Texas singer who went by the name the legendary Stardust cowboy."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: The Surprising History of Glam Rock

xref.title: The Thin White Duke Persona - Thomas Jerome Newton Influence
xref.body: This amoral, hollow, damaged, and emotionless character, with his signature white shirt and waistcoat, emerged from an autobiography Bowie began while filming "The Man Who Fell to Earth," in which he played the doomed space alien Thomas Jerome Newton. Bowie loved the character and asked to keep the costuming, directly influencing his look for the next couple of years. "This character came from a sort of autobiography Bowie had begun while filming the man who fell to Earth, the movie where he played a doomed space alien named Thomas Jerome Newton."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

xref.title: Tim Commerford's Background and Influences
xref.body: Tim Commerford, known by various names including Tim Bob and Tim C, grew up in Irvine, south of Los Angeles. His mother was a mathematician and his father an aeronautical engineer who worked on the space shuttle. He and Zack de la Rocha formed their first band, Juvenile Expression, in grade seven, after Zack taught Tim to play bass using the Sex Pistols' "Never Mind the Bollocks" album. Tim also spent hours learning Geddy Lee's bass parts from Rush albums. "Mom was a mathematician while his dad was an aeronautical engineer who actually worked on the space shuttle."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

xref.title: Tom Morello's Guitar Style
xref.body: By the release of The Battle of Los Angeles, Tom Morello had developed a highly unique guitar playing style. He was known for using numerous effects to create diverse sounds, but a key characteristic highlighted was "the space between the notes," where "short gaps of nothing between the notes often say more than riffs that don't have gaps," creating a powerful effect. "By this time, he had developed a very unique playing style. He used lots of effects to get lots of different sounds. But when you listen to Tom's playing, the thing that really gets me is the space between the notes."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

xref.title: Tony Iommi's Influence on Restraint
xref.body: He studied old Black Sabbath records to observe how Tony Iommi effectively used restraint, recognizing the importance of the "space between the notes" in his playing. "He also spent a lot of time listening to old black Sabbath records, noting how guitarist Tony Iomey often exhibited restraint, utilizing that the space between the notes could be as important as the notes themselves."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

xref.title: Tour Bus Bunk Description
xref.body: Arion Salazar describes the bunks on a tour bus as small, coffin-like compartments. These bunks have curtains that can be pulled and buttoned shut, creating a "little cocoon" that serves as a private space for band members, likened to the "hellbop" concept. "We're in these little things that are like coffins, the curtains you pull them shut and button them shut and you're like securing your little cocoon."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

xref.title: Transition to "Blue-Eyed Plastic Soul"
xref.body: During the "Diamond Dogs" tour, Bowie began transitioning from his "spaceman" image to a more elegant, sophisticated look with shorter hair and tailored suits. This paralleled a shift in his musical interests towards American soul and R&B, leading to the smoother, funkier sound of "Young Americans." This endorsement of black music encouraged many of his fans to explore those genres. "Bowie became less space man and more elegant, shorter hair, tailored suits, an air of sophistication."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

xref.title: Transition to "Elegant" Persona
xref.body: During the "Diamond Dogs" tour, fans observed Bowie undergoing a transition, moving from his "spaceman" image to a more elegant aesthetic. This included shorter hair, tailored suits, and an overall air of sophistication, reflecting a shift in both his personal style and musical direction towards American soul and R&B. "Bowie became less space man and more elegant. Elder hair, tailored suits and this air of sophistication."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

xref.title: Transition to Producer – Madison Indie Scene
xref.body: After playing in bands like Spooner (three albums) and Firetown (one album), Butch Vig developed a keen interest in producing music. He established a small studio space in Madison, Wisconsin, where he began working with local indie groups, including Killdozer. "It was around this time that butch became interested in producing music So he ran into small space in Madison, Wisconsin Where he began working with local indie groups including a group called Killdozer."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

xref.title: Victorian Jail Rehearsal Space
xref.body: Following a police raid on their previous rehearsal space, "The Chateau," the band moved their operations to a building that had once served as an old Victorian jail. This move continued their pattern of choosing ironically artsy locations for their creative endeavors. "The cops weren't so sympathetic though. They raided the place, necessitating a move to a building that was once an old Victorian jail."
